rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A function f: A -> B assigns to every element of A exactly one element of B, where A is the domain and B the codomain, while the range is the set of outputs actually attained. Injective (one-to-one), surjective (onto) and bijective describe how far the outputs avoid collisions and cover the codomain, and only a bijective function has an inverse f^-1, satisfying f^-1(f(x)) = x and f(f^-1(y)) = y, whose graph is the…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: x Every function has an inverse. x Only bijective functions have inverses.  ·  x f^-1(x) = 1/f(x). x f^-1 is the inverse function, not reciprocal.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: For f(x) = 1/(x-3) the domain is every real x except 3, and the range is every real y except 0, because 0 is never attained.  ·  x^2 on all of R is not one-to-one and so has no inverse; only the branch x >= 0, or x <= 0, does.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Find the domain and range of f(x) = 1/(x-3).  ·  If f(x) = 2x + 5, find f^-1(x).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: x Domain = Range always. x They can be different sets.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Find the domain and the range of a given function, naming the restriction imposed by every radical, denominator and logarithm.  ·  Construct the inverse of a function by writing y = f(x), solving for x in terms of y, then interchanging x and y, and state the domain and range of the inverse.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: If any horizontal line cuts the graph twice, f is not one-to-one and f^-1 does not exist, so stop immediately.  ·  To sketch the inverse, swap the coordinates of a few known points instead of redoing the algebra from scratch.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Find the domain and the range of f(x) = 1/(x - 3).  ·  If f(x) = 2x + 5, find f^-1(x) and state its domain and range.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Usually a 2-mark question with one mark for the domain and one for the range, and the restriction on x must be written as an explicit inequality.  ·  Inverse computation is typically a 5-mark question, and sketching a function together with its inverse is a standard 5-mark graph question.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Domain: the set of all inputs x for which f is defined; range: the set of all output values f actually produces.  ·  The codomain is the declared target B, while the range is only the subset of B that is actually hit by f.  ·  Injective (one-to-one): different inputs give different outputs, tested by the horizontal line test on the graph.  ·  Surjective (onto): every element of the codomain is the image of at least one input.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: f^-1 denotes the inverse function, never the reciprocal 1/f(x).  ·  Domain and range are generally different sets; the range of f is the domain of f^-1.  ·  An inverse exists only for a bijective function, so a restriction is often needed first, as with x^2 on x >= 0.  ·  Composition does not commute, since f o g and g o f are different functions in general.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Show that f(x) = x^3 is one-to-one on R and find f^-1(x).  ·  If f(x) = (x + 1)/(x - 1), evaluate f o f and deduce whether f^-1 = f.  ·  Find the domain of the composite function f o g for f(x) = sqrt(2 - x) and g(x) = x^2 - 1.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: MCQs repeatedly test the distinction between f^-1(x) and 1/f(x), and the false claim that every function has an inverse.  ·  Composite function questions in 5 and 10-mark sets often ask for the domain of f o g, which needs g to be defined and the range of g to lie inside the domain of f.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: What is the domain of f(x) = sqrt(x - 2)? → B  ·  If f(x) = 2x + 5, then f^-1(x) is → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 1. Function Definition  ·  A function f from set A to set B is a rule that assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B. Written as f: A -> B, where A is the domain and B is the codomain.  ·  ### 2. Domain and Range

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Bijective = injective + surjective; only a bijective function has an inverse f^-1: B -> A.  ·  Composite function (f o g)(x) = f(g(x)); composition is associative but not commutative.  ·  Solving f(x) = k for x is the same work as finding f^-1(k), so the two skills are really one skill.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: For f(x) = (x+1)/(x-1) one finds f(f(x)) = x, so the function is its own inverse and f^-1 = f.  ·  A constant function on a set with more than one element is onto its image but not one-to-one, so it has no inverse.  ·  Restricting the domain of f shrinks its range, and that is exactly what can turn it into the whole codomain and create an inverse.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A function f from set A to set B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B, and is written f: A -> B with domain A and codomain B.  ·  For f(x) = sqrt(x-2) the domain is x >= 2 and the range is y >= 0, because a square root is never negative.  ·  If f: A -> B is bijective then f^-1 exists with f^-1(f(x)) = x and f(f^-1(y)) = y, so (f o f^-1)(x) = (f^-1 o f)(x) = x.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The graph of f^-1 is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x, so the point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f^-1.  ·  For f(x) = ax + b with a != 0 the inverse is f^-1(x) = (x - b)/a, and the branch f(x) = x^2 restricted to x >= 0 has inverse f^-1(x) = sqrt(x).  ·  Replace x by y, solve for x, then swap back: the three-step recipe works for every invertible function.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Verify the answer with f^-1(f(x)) = x; the result must come out to exactly x, never to a constant.  ·  If the solved expression for x is the original formula with x and y exchanged, then f = f^-1.  ·  Determine the range of f(x) = (x - 1)^2 + 3 restricted to x >= 0.
